n_TOF EAR2 · X17 scintillators · the first microseconds after the γ-flash

When a MIP is seen after the γ-flash, and how much of that rests on real pulses

Plastics from ~0.8 µs; SiPM walls ~4 µs at dedicated intensity, ~3 µs at parasitic. The efficiency comes from injected pulses, so it is only quoted where real pulses show the electronics to be linear

0.8 µs

plastic

A MIP is seen ≥ 90 % from 0.8 µs (dedicated). Real pulses respond linearly from 0.4 µs. Energy: gain measured from 2.0 µs, σ(E)/E ≈ 20% at 2–3 µs; before, the gain is only bounded (0.21–0.53).

4.0 µs

SiPM wall (one end)

Per bar end, dedicated; parasitic 3.2 µs. Real pulses respond linearly from 2.5 µs (spectra and bar ends). A 1-MIP end pulse stays poorly measured at dedicated intensity: σ(E)/E ≈ 44%, σ(t) ≈ 3 ns at 10 µs (pile-up).

—

liquid

Not a lepton counter here: no MIP reference. A linear response is not established on real pulses (dedicated and parasitic spectra differ by 10–20 % even at 60 µs). Injection-only numbers: appendix.

MIP = the measured cosmic-muon spectrum of each counter. Dedicated pulses (8.5×10¹² protons), time since the flash. 3,517 bunches of 180 production runs.

1

Details

This version answers two concerns with the previous one. (1) The injection test adds pulses to the recorded traces, so it assumes the electronics are still linear after the flash and is a best case. Linearity is now tested on real pulses alone (slides 5–7), and the efficiency is only used where that test passes. (2) Results were shown as series of injected pulse sizes. They are now folded with the measured MIP spectrum: how often a MIP is lost, and how well it is measured.

"Seen" = the pulse is found at its time. "Usable" = seen ≥ 90 % in every bin up to 40 µs, and from the time real pulses show a linear response. Correction found while reworking: the energy uncertainty of the previous version added the gain uncertainty in absolute instead of relative units, understating σ(E) at low gain by up to ×3 (7 % at 2 µs became 17–20 %).

What a pulse has to be found on: the first 10 µs of one dedicated bunch

Recorded traces (min–max per 8 ns) with ~1-MIP pulses added every µs (diamonds: green = reconstructed within ±50 %, red = lost or off); plastic 200 mV, liquid 100 mV, wall end 30 mV

2

Details

Plastics and liquids: saturated for ~0.2 µs, then a dense train of fast-neutron recoils peaking at ~1 µs (2 MeV neutrons at 19.5 m), falling to a few tens of mV by 5 µs. A pulse on that slope is found and fitted with a local baseline. Walls: switched off by the divert gate until ~0.65 µs, then the stored flash charge clips the amplifier at ~1 V until ~1.6 µs and decays over ~10 µs, with a continuous rain of 10–60 mV pulses on it. That rain, not the tail, is what spoils the wall reconstruction.

Run 224712, from early.py --examples.

3

Details

A MIP (minimum-ionizing particle: a cosmic muon here, an X17 e± in the experiment) loses ~2 MeV per cm of plastic, so ≈ 4 MeV in the 20 mm plastic bar and 0.47 MeV in the 3 mm wall bar. The deposit fluctuates (Landau) and the light collection adds a spread, so the pulse size is a distribution ~40 % wide: the efficiency for a MIP is the efficiency per size averaged over this distribution.

The plastic coincidences also contain a shoulder of small pulses (grey, 15–33 % per bar): tracks that clip the edge of the bar. An X17 lepton from the target crosses the whole bar, so only the fitted through-going peak is used. For the walls the per-end size is the measured spectrum, all positions along the bar.

What the earlier series were: injected pulse sizes in mV (plastic 25–800, wall 8–120, liquid 25–400), labelled in MeVee or in MIP. MeVee is the light an electron of that energy would make (the appendix keeps that scale, anchored at 3.45 MeVee for the median of all coincidences, shoulder included). The MIP results fold the per-size efficiencies with this spectrum, after multiplying every size by the measured gain: at 2–3 µs a dedicated plastic MIP makes ~70 mV, not ~215 mV.

What the injected pulses can and cannot tell

An injected pulse is added to the recorded trace: it tests the algorithm and the pile-up with the real beam pulses, never how the detector and electronics respond to light after the flash

quantitymeasured withassumes
is the pulse found? (efficiency)injectionlinear superposition
reconstructed amplitude ÷ true (response, ±7 %)injectionlinear superposition
spread of the amplitude from pile-upinjectionlinear superposition
time resolutioninjection; walls checked on real bar endslinear superposition
PMT / SiPM gain (plastic ×3 low at 2–3 µs)real pulses: spectrum scalesame particles at both times
is the response linear?real pulses: spectrum shape, bar endssee slides 5–7
MIP size distributionreal pulses: cosmic muonsmuon angles ≈ lepton angles

Injection is the best case: if the PMT, SiPM, amplifier or digitizer were non-linear after the flash (a compression, a baseline-dependent gain, a slower pulse), real pulses would do worse than injected ones, and the test could not see it.

So linearity is tested on real pulses only, and the injection numbers are only used where that test passes: plastics from 0.4 µs, walls from 2.5 µs. Before that, they are shaded grey.

4

Details

Within that, the injection does more than exercise the algorithm: the pulses sit on the real flash tail of every bunch, among the real beam-induced pulses, so the losses and the spread it measures are the pile-up of this beam. A found fraction near 100 % for large pulses is expected and says little; the useful output is how the efficiency and the spread fall for small pulses as the pile-up density changes.

A pure gain change is a linear response (every pulse scaled by the same factor). It is invisible to the injection and is measured from the real spectra instead (slide 8).

5

Details

The test. A response that is linear up to a gain multiplies every amplitude by the same factor, so the spectrum keeps its shape. A non-linear response changes the shape: a compression of large pulses pulls the 99 % point in more than the median. Per channel and time bin, the spectrum of isolated real pulses (template fit, above 20 mV plastics/liquids, 15 mV walls) is fitted as a scaled copy of a reference, with the threshold applied consistently, and the mismatch of the 50/75/90/95/99 % points is kept; median over channels.

Two references. Dedicated against parasitic at the same time: the particles per proton are the same, only the flash is twice as large, so a flash-driven non-linearity shows while a change of particle mix cannot. Against the same intensity at 20–60 µs: valid only once the particles are the same capture-γ e± (from ~2.5 µs). Plastics: dedicated and parasitic agree in shape within 1–8 % from 0.4 µs, while their scale differs by ×0.3–0.7 (the dedicated gain is lower). Walls: the shapes differ by 30–45 % until 2.2 µs (the amplifier recovering from clipping) and agree within 2–5 % from 2.5 µs. Liquids: 10–20 % at every time to 60 µs, long after the flash, so the cause is probably not the flash (different run conditions behind the two intensities are possible), but linearity is not established.

What it cannot see. A non-linearity that is the same for both intensities (the dedicated vs parasitic test), or one that a change of particle mix happens to cancel. The amplitude range tested is the 50–99 % points: 30–90 mV (plastics at 0.5 µs), 45–210 mV (walls), which contains the MIP pulse at the sagged gain. Code: linearity.py.

6

Details

Plastic 4:2 at 0.6 µs: its dedicated pulses are 0.70 of the parasitic ones, and once scaled the two spectra lie on each other: the larger flash lowers the gain without changing the shape. Wall 3:2 at 1.8 µs: the dedicated spectrum is narrower (fewer large pulses, more medium ones), which a scale cannot produce: the amplifier is still recovering from clipping. Wall 3:6 at 3.5 µs: they agree again, at a scale of 1.21; the dedicated/parasitic wall scale stays ~1.1 to 60 µs, so that offset is not a flash effect.

The slide before uses the median over channels of exactly this comparison.

7

Details

The two ends of a bar have different SiPM gains and so ride on different flash tails. If the gain of the electronics depended on the tail level, their ratio at a fixed position would move while the tails decay. It moves by ≤ 1 % from 2.5 µs (±3 % bar to bar), and by up to 4 % at 0.3–2 µs with a 7–24 % bar-to-bar scatter. The end-to-end time difference keeps its position within 0.2 ns from 2.5 µs; its spread is 3.3 / 2.8 ns at 3 / 5 µs against 2.5 ns late, and 3.5–11 ns before 2.5 µs. This is the only test of timing on real pulses: the plastic timing is from the injection alone.

Pairs within ±30 ns, accidentals from a 500 ns shifted window subtracted. Both ends share the flash, so a non-linearity common to both ends cancels here; the spectrum test on the previous slides covers that.

8

Details

From 2 µs every plastic pulse above threshold is a capture-γ e±, so the scale of the spectrum against its late value is the gain (all quantiles move together, slide 5). Before 2 µs the pulses are fast-neutron recoils, whose spectrum has another shape, so the scale alone is not a gain. Two bounds remain. Below: the 99 % point against its late value (recoils are softer than capture γ, so this underestimates the gain). Above, for dedicated bunches: the dedicated/parasitic scale of the linearity test, since the dedicated gain is that factor times the parasitic gain and the parasitic gain is at most 1. Dedicated: 0.20–0.32 at 0.5–0.8 µs, 0.21–0.64 at 0.8–1.6 µs. Parasitic: from the 99 % point up to 1.

Walls: the spectrum scale is 1.05–1.18 at 2.5–10 µs against 20–60 µs, but the same 1.14 holds between dedicated and parasitic to 60 µs, so it is not taken as a gain; gain 1 with the spread as uncertainty.

9

Details

For every time bin, each MIP of the measured spectrum makes a pulse of its size (mV, at the late gain) × the gain; the injected-pulse efficiency at that size (interpolated between the injected sizes) is averaged over the spectrum and over the counters. "Seen": the reconstruction finds a pulse at its time. "Within ±50 %": its amplitude is usable.

Plastics: early the whole spectrum is pushed down by the gain (at 0.5–0.7 µs a dedicated MIP makes ~55 mV) and its low side drops into the pile-up. Within ±50 % is what the capture-γ pile-up spoils at 5–20 µs: the dashed curve stays at 0.92 (dedicated) and 0.96 (parasitic). Walls: a ~35 mV, 500 ns end pulse under the rain of real pulses; the parasitic intensity halves the rain.

The fraction of MIPs below the smallest injected size (extrapolated): ≤ 2 % from 4 µs on the plastics, up to 10 % at 0.5–0.7 µs (dedicated). Code: mip_eff.py.

How well a MIP is measured: plastic σ(E)/E ≈ 20 % and σ(t) ≈ 0.5 ns at 2–5 µs; a wall end ~40–60 % and 2–5 ns

Details

The previous version quoted these for a 200 mV pulse at every time. At 2–3 µs a dedicated plastic MIP is ~70 mV because of the gain, and a smaller pulse has a larger relative spread under the same pile-up, so the MIP numbers are worse: σ(E)/E 20 % (11–13 % pile-up, 15–17 % gain) and σ(t) 0.4–0.5 ns. Before 2 µs the gain range dominates (±50 %). From ~10 µs, 13–14 % dedicated and 7–8 % parasitic.

Walls, one end, a MIP: 37–60 % and 2.3–5 ns at dedicated intensity from 4.5 µs, 13–26 % and 0.9–2.3 ns parasitic, from the injection; the real bar ends (previous slide) give 3.3 → 2.5 ns for the end-to-end difference at 3 µs → late, for the whole spectrum of sizes.

What this means for a measurement in the first microseconds

From the 2026 data; for this apparatus at 4 and 8.5×10¹² protons per pulse

Plastics see a MIP from ~0.8 µs and respond linearly from 0.4 µs, but the PMT gain is ×3–5 low in the first µs (dedicated) and is only bounded before 2 µs. A light-pulser gain monitor firing in the first µs would turn the ±50 % energy scale before 2 µs into a measurement; a base built for high anode current would shrink the sag itself and raise the early MIP pulse out of the pile-up.

SiPM walls are not linear until ~2.5 µs (the amplifier recovers from clipping), and after that a 1-MIP end pulse sits in the pile-up of real pulses: ≥ 90 % seen from ~4 µs at dedicated intensity, but measured within ±50 % only 64–77 % of the time. Faster shaping (shorter pulses) is the lever: the pile-up probability scales with the pulse length.

Liquids: no MIP reference, and their linearity is not established on real pulses.

Everything early scales with intensity: at parasitic intensity the plastic gain loss halves and a wall end sees a MIP ≥ 90 % from ~3 µs.

12

What this does not rule out

· The efficiency, the reconstruction response, the pile-up spread and the plastic timing come from injected pulses and assume linear superposition. Real pulses support that from 0.4 µs (plastics) and 2.5 µs (walls), within ~10 % in spectrum shape. A non-linearity equal at both intensities, or one a change of particle mix cancels, is not excluded.

· Before 2 µs the plastic gain is bounded (dedicated 0.2–0.64), not measured: energies there are uncertain by ~±50 %.

· The plastic timing is not tested on real pulses (no partner of sub-ns resolution); the wall timing is, on bar ends.

· The MIP spectrum is cosmic muons at an angle; a lepton at normal incidence makes a slightly smaller pulse, so the efficiencies are slightly optimistic for the walls, where the MIP sits at the edge of the pile-up. The plastic spectrum is the fitted through-going peak; counting the clipping-track shoulder as MIPs would lower the efficiencies.

· Liquids: linearity not established, no energy scale; their injection numbers (appendix) are a best case.

· Pile-up scales with the pulse rate: these numbers hold for this apparatus and these intensities.

16

Details

Reconstruction response: median A_fit/A of injected pulses over the same before the flash. Within ±7 % for the plastics from 0.4 µs and the liquids from 0.45 µs; the walls read 25–50 % low at 2–3.5 µs (a pulse on the falling stored-charge tail and under the pile-up) and within 3 % from ~4.5 µs.

Gain: plastics from the 99 % point of the measured spectrum on a fine time grid (×1.12 bins), capped at 1; uncertainty = half the difference between the singles and the pulses behind a wall hit ⊕ 3 %. Dedicated: 0.33 at 2–3 µs, 0.43 / 0.61 / 0.76 / 0.86 / 0.95 at 3.5 / 4.5 / 5.6 / 7 / 9 µs, 1.0 by 11 µs; parasitic 0.56–0.73 at 2–3 µs, 0.9 by 4 µs. The sag scales with intensity, as an anode-current-driven PMT gain loss does. Before 2 µs the plastic spectrum is fast-neutron recoils and its shape cannot separate gain from mix (q99 gives only ≥ 0.15–0.3). Walls: no sag resolved (1 ± 3–7 %). Liquids: their spectrum changes ×1.4–2.9 in shape, no reference.

17

Details

After dividing by response × gain, what is left is (1) the spread of the reconstructed amplitude, which pile-up with the beam pulses sets and no correction removes, and (2) the uncertainty of the correction: the gain uncertainty, the statistical error of the response, and half the change of the correction across a time bin. Plastics, ~1 MIP, dedicated: σ(E)/E 18% at 2.2 µs, 16% at 2.8 µs, 20% at 3.5 µs, 18% at 4.5 µs, 15% at 5.6 µs, 14% at 7.1 µs, 14% at 8.9 µs, 14% at 11 µs, 14% at 14 µs, 13% at 18 µs, 13% at 22 µs, 12% at 28 µs. The best window is 2–3 µs, between the end of the fast-neutron train and the start of the dense capture-γ pile-up. Note the gain uncertainty is relative: it weighs ×3 more where the gain is 0.33.

Liquids: no energy scale, the reconstruction spread alone is shown.

Per size: time resolution (injection only)

σ68 of t_fit − t₀ after removing the median offset (hover: offset), dedicated; red = the limit used for "reliable". Colours by size, thick = reference signal

18

Details

The median offset (time bias) is below 0.05 ns for plastics and liquids after 0.4 µs and below 0.3 ns for the walls after 3 µs; it is corrected the same way as the amplitude. The resolution is the jitter from noise and pile-up on the leading edge; before the flash it is 0.07 ns (plastics, liquids, 1-ns sampling with a sub-ns fit) and 0.4 ns (walls). Plastic ~1 MIP, dedicated: 0.49 ns at 0.4 µs, 0.39 ns at 0.6 µs, 0.33 ns at 0.7 µs, 0.27 ns at 0.9 µs, 0.21 ns at 1.1 µs, 0.16 ns at 1.4 µs, 0.14 ns at 1.8 µs, 0.14 ns at 2.2 µs, 0.18 ns at 2.8 µs, 0.23 ns at 3.5 µs, 0.28 ns at 4.5 µs, 0.31 ns at 5.6 µs, 0.31 ns at 7.1 µs, 0.30 ns at 8.9 µs, 0.29 ns at 11 µs, 0.28 ns at 14 µs, 0.26 ns at 18 µs, 0.24 ns at 22 µs, 0.22 ns at 28 µs.

The flash time itself (PKUP + per-detector constant) is known to ~10 ns between detector families; within a family it cancels.

19

Details

The efficiency of a pulse of a given size (found within ±50 % of its response), interpolated in the size. For the plastics the energy threshold divides by the gain: a sagging PMT makes every deposit smaller, so at 2–3 µs (gain 0.33, dedicated) the 90 % threshold is ~2.5 MeVee against ~0.8 MeVee in amplitude terms. Walls: 90 % only above ~1.2–1.5 MeV (2.5–3 MIP per end) at dedicated intensity up to ~10 µs; half of 1-MIP pulses are kept from ~4 µs. Where a curve is missing the threshold is outside the injected range (below the smallest or above the largest size).

Method: injection for the reconstruction, the spectra for the gain

3,517 bunches of 180 production runs; every number split by beam intensity

real flash trace

every channel, every bunch: the unsuppressed block, 10 µs before to 40–250 µs after the flash

→

+ pulses of known size

family template, known amplitude and time; a comb every 0.6–2 µs; clipped at saturation

→

reconstruct

peak finder → template fit with every neighbour and a local baseline (multi-pulse fit)

→

compare

found? A_fit / A? t_fit − t₀? The same 1.5–8 µs before the flash is the reference

Injection measures the electronics and the algorithm on the real tail: baseline, clipping, pulse shape, and pile-up with the real beam pulses. It gives the efficiency, the reconstruction response and its spread, and the timing.

It cannot see a gain change in the PMT/SiPM (the pulse is added after it). The gain comes from the measured amplitude spectra: a gain change scales all their quantiles together, a change of particle mix does not (appendix).

20

Details

Amplitudes injected: plastics 25–800 mV (0.45–14 MeVee), wall ends 8–120 mV (0.3–4 MIP), liquids 25–400 mV. Energy scale: plastics 56 mV/MeVee on average (39–72 per bar, muon calibration and cosmics at 30–32 ms); wall ends 28 mV per MIP (22–31), a MIP being 0.47 MeV in 3 mm. Liquids: no energy scale.

Code: inject.py (condor), early.py, gain_ref.py.

Fast-neutron recoils until ~2 µs, then capture γ: the population settles early

Geant4, 5×10⁸ EAR2 neutrons (1 meV–100 MeV) on the n_TOF apparatus, light with Birks quenching

SiPM wall

plastic

liquid

data

22

Details

At 19.5 m a neutron arriving 1 µs after the flash has ~2 MeV; at 2 µs ~0.5 MeV. Its proton recoils then give less than 0.1 MeVee (quenching), so from ~2 µs everything above threshold is e± from γ: capture γ in the apparatus (hydrogen 2.2 MeV dominates in the simulation). In the simulation the deposit spectrum keeps one shape from ~2 µs to ~1 ms (95 % quantile 1.99 MeVee, the 2.2 MeV Compton edge), then hardens slightly.

Rates: the simulation is within ×0.6 of the data on the plastics at 3–300 µs (Geant4 / data = 1.77) but ×5 low after 1 ms, and its spectrum is softer than the data (data 95 % quantile behind a wall hit 4.6–5.3 MeVee, simulation ~2 MeVee). Not simulated: the experimental hall (room-return neutrons, captures in concrete and the dump), the in-beam γ of the spallation target, the flash itself. The beam profile is the pre-2026-10-14 one (5× too narrow). So Geant4 explains what arrives early, not all of what arrives late.

Code: g4_mix.py (condor over full_sim/neutrons_fullrange), g4_mix_analysis.py.

Gain or particle mix? A gain change moves every quantile together

Quantiles of the amplitude spectrum over their 1–10 ms values. Plastics: all drop together before ~10 µs (a gain sag); later q50 and q99 are back, q75–q95 stay low to ~0.3 ms (the mix)

median (q50)

q75

q90

q95

q99 = the gain estimate

±5 %

23

Details

The earlier note read the 95 % edge of the plastic spectrum behind a wall hit as an upper bound on the gain sag (0.71 / 0.87 / 0.93 at 10 / 100 / 300 µs). The quantiles separate the two: from ~20 µs the median and the 99 % point are back within 2–4 % while the 75–95 % points are still 10–20 % low; a gain sag cannot do that, a change in the share of 2–5 MeVee pulses can. Before ~10 µs all five drop by the same factor (0.37 at 3 µs, ~0.6 at 5 µs, ~0.8 at 8 µs), which is what a gain sag looks like. A PMT whose base is drained by the ~0.5 V of pile-up current in the first µs behaves this way.

Walls: the top of the spectrum is within 1.07–1.00 from 3 µs on (a few % above 1 early: piled pulses are bigger), and dips 3 % at 0.2–1 ms. No gain sag the data can resolve beyond that. Liquids: their quantiles move by ×1.4–2.9 at 2–100 µs, so the shape changes far too much to read a gain from them.

Caveat: this assumes the top of the spectrum is made by the same particles at all times; the simulation says the population is capture γ from ~2 µs, but it does not reproduce the hardest part of the data spectrum.

Code: gain_ref.py.

Most of the loss is pile-up with real beam pulses; a clean pulse is unbiased after a few µs

Left: chance that a real pulse ≥ 5 % of the injected one sits within a pulse width. Right: amplitude bias of the injected pulses that have no such neighbour

plastic

parasitic

±3 %

24

Details

The pile-up probability is the beam-induced occupancy: the pulse rate times the pulse width. It falls with the rate, roughly in proportion to the beam intensity (dashed = parasitic, half the protons). It is not a property of the flash and does not go away with better electronics; a narrower pulse or a multi-pulse fit (used here) reduces what it costs.

Clean pulses are rare where the occupancy is high, so their points start late on the walls and plastics; points with fewer than 100 clean pulses are not drawn.

Details

Every curve stops where the unsuppressed head block ends (walls ~40 µs, liquids 20–150 µs, plastics ~200 µs): only there is the full trace recorded, so only there can a pulse be injected. After it, the zero-suppression keeps blocks around pulses, and the rate (slide 3) is what changes.

The losses are mostly pile-up: a real pulse within a pulse width that pulls the fitted amplitude. The fraction of pulses with such a neighbour is on the next slide; on clean pulses alone the reconstruction is already unbiased within a few µs.

Beyond the recorded head block: the accurate fraction follows the pulse rate

Injection (points) and exp(−a × measured pulse rate) fitted to it (dashed), carried to 10 ms with the measured rate; vertical: where the model reaches 90 %

dedicated

parasitic

injection

model

≥ 90 %

26

Details

If a pulse is spoiled only by a neighbour arriving at random, the fraction left intact is exp(−a R) with R the pulse rate per channel and a an effective width (µs). a is fitted on the injection bins after the tail itself has stopped mattering (walls ≥ 10 µs, plastics and liquids ≥ 5 µs), with R the measured rate of pulses above 4 mV in the same channels and bunches; fit residuals 0.02–0.05 for ~1 MIP. The rate is measured to 10 ms, so the model reaches times the injection cannot. Fitted a (~1 MIP): liquid ded 0.008 µs; liquid par 0.005 µs; plastic ded 0.025 µs; plastic par 0.014 µs; SiPM wall (per end) ded 0.501 µs; SiPM wall (per end) par 0.298 µs.

Energy bias = reconstruction × gain: the plastics are low by tens of % before ~10 µs, ≤ 4 % after ~20 µs

Median bias of reconstructed ~1-MIP pulses (thin), detector gain from the data (dashed), their product (thick)

dedicated

parasitic

reconstruction

±3 %

27

Details

Reconstruction bias: median A_fit/A of the injected pulses over the same before the flash (all pulses, pile-up included, multi-pulse fit). Gain: q99 of the spectrum (previous slide), plastics behind a wall hit and wall bars; the liquids have none. The total is the bias of a reconstructed energy if nothing is corrected. Both parts are smooth in time and measured, so a correction g(t) can be applied; what remains is its uncertainty, ~the spread between the plastic populations (coincident vs singles, ~0.1 at 5–8 µs, < 0.03 after 15 µs).
